summary.text:
Harlow District Council's Provisional Outturn 2025/26 to Cabinet on 9 July 2026, a 12-page revenue-and-capital report for noting. Deliberately brief for the shape of paper it is — many district outturns run to 30 or 40 pages. Executive summary and recommendations set out a £39,000 General Fund surplus (third consecutive year), a £4.940m planned use of Housing Revenue Account balances, and combined capital delivery of £111.631m across the Non-Housing (£35.069m) and Housing (£76.562m) Capital Programmes. Reserves position is strong: GF working balance £4.008m against a £2.5m minimum, HRA working balance £9.976m against a £2m minimum, earmarked reserves £35.399m total.

The report carries no treasury section. No CFR, no external borrowing total, no PWLB loan-book table, no maturity profile, no prudential indicators, no MRP policy statement, no LOBO or LA-lending detail — those all live in the Statement of Accounts 2025/26 whose Appendix (the actual accounts) is not on disk, only its 5-page covering paper (s30996). Every debt-side number in the outturn sits inside a General Fund or HRA variance table.

Those inside-the-table numbers are the treasury story of the paper, and they are real. Net Interest Payable on the General Fund came in at £1.146m against a £558k budget — a shade over twice budget; the HRA interest charges line came in £1.167m adverse (£9.496m against £8.329m). Combined £1.755m over budget on debt service across the two accounts, roughly 20% adverse on the combined £8.887m budget. Paragraph 22 attributes the HRA piece specifically to 'higher financing costs associated with the capital programme', which reads consistently with £55.513m of prudential borrowing drawn during the year across the two capital tables (£14.519m NHCP, £40.994m HCP). The Debt Financing earmarked reserve at Appendix A is the piece that connects the two — £3.000m opening, £570k drawn in year, £2.430m closing. On the current rate of draw the reserve carries about four years.

Loan-book reconciliation cannot be run against this paper — no loan book is printed. Our price_book returns 10 PWLB loans totalling £251.837m at 3.7716% weighted at 31/3/26, with a live view of 14 loans totalling £267.145m dominated by four £41.767m loans at 3.21-3.50% maturing 28 March in 2030, 2034, 2038 and 2042 (a single HRA-vintage tranche of ~£167m, 63% of the current book). Per PIPELINE.md, no loan-book claim is made in the email. The balance-sheet identity check similarly cannot be closed — every left-hand-side term is absent from the paper.

Email drafted around two hooks the paper does support: the interest-variance itself and the Debt Financing reserve mechanism carrying it. No advice, no comparison numbers, no reconciliation claim. Bridge opening compliments the paper's brevity (genuine — 12 pages for a stock-owning district's outturn is unusual). S151 title on record: Jan Willis, Interim Director Finance and Section 151 Officer (confirmed from the draft SoA covering paper s30996 p.4; the outturn itself only prints the title, not the name). No email address is published in either paper on disk; recipient line will be blocked until an address is added.

officer.body:
Dear Jan,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a couple of thoughts on the Provisional Outturn taken to Cabinet on 9 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Most district outturns we read run to 30 or 40 pages; yours does the job in 12 without dropping any of it, and that made it a straightforward read.

The line that caught our eye is the debt-financing variance flagged in the General Fund bullets on page 5. Net Interest Payable came in at £1.146m on a budget of £558k, so a shade over twice budget on the General Fund alone. Add the £1.167m adverse on HRA interest charges at paragraph 21 and it's about £1.755m over budget on debt service across the two accounts, on a combined budget of £8.887m — around 20% adverse. Paragraph 22 attributes the HRA piece to 'higher financing costs associated with the capital programme', which reads consistently with the £55.5m of prudential borrowing drawn during the year across the two capital tables at pages 9 and 10 (£14.519m on the NHCP, £40.994m on the HCP).

The Debt Financing earmarked reserve at Appendix A is the piece that connects the two: £3.000m at 31 March 2025, £570k drawn in year, £2.430m at 31 March 2026. At the current rate of draw the reserve carries about four years, which is broadly the horizon over which any residual borrowing programme is likely to keep landing new interest cost. We publish PWLB rates at both fixings on the front of pwlbtoday.org, and price every published council's PWLB book daily against the DMO's premature repayment curve at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis — indicative only, and only the DMO can quote.

One standing point because CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put it in front of every S151: the liability benchmark pathway becomes central to how the whole treasury strategy is framed. Interactive version of it, tied to our rate feeds, is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

On training, three fit the paper. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice is the obvious one given where CIPFA is going. MRP — policy options and revenue impact sits behind the £1.827m MRP outturn line at the General Fund table. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator is the one to name if any rescheduling thinking comes up. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if any of it is useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Provisional Outturn Report 2025/26, Cabinet 9 July 2026, at https://Harlow.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s31016/outturn-report-2025-26.pdf, together with the Earmarked Reserves appendix (s31017) on the same agenda.
